notes.text: I will sow — That is, I will exceedingly multiply them, both with men and with cattle.

Behold — And not only with the Jews, but all those who should be ingrafted into that Olive. It is not called the new covenant, because it was as to the substance new, for it was made with Abraham, Gen. xvii, 7, and with the Jews, Deut. xxvi, 17, 18, but because it was revealed after a new manner, more fully and particularly, plainly and clearly. Nor was the ceremonial law any part of it, as it was to the Jews, a strict observance of that. It was likewise new in regard of the efficacy of the spirit attending it, in a much fuller and larger manner.

Not according — The covenant which God made with the Jews when they came out of the land of Egypt, was on God's part the law which he gave them, with the promises annexed; on their part (which made it a formal covenant) their promise of obedience to it.

With — That is, with those who are Jews inwardly. And write it - The prophet's design is here to express the difference betwixt the law and the gospel. The first shews duty, the latter brings the grace of regeneration, by which the heart is changed, and enabled for duty. All under the time of the law that came to salvation, were saved by this new covenant; but this was not evidently exhibited; neither was the regenerating grace of God so common under the time of the law, as it hath been under the gospel.
I will forgive — God makes the root of all this grace to be the free pardon, and the remission of their sins.

glossa.text: *Behold the days come saith the Lord.* All promises of this kind, etc., *as far as* but that God may be all in all.
*The teeth shall be set on edge. ((ID.))* The teeth of those who eat cannot feel sweetness, etc., *as far as* not by the harshness of the foods, but by the fault of the teeth.
*Behold the days.* By this testimony Paul, etc., *as far as* and that circumcision and the sabbath might be spiritually fulfilled.

*And he shall not teach.* That they may not seek Jewish masters and the commandments of men, but may be taught by the Holy Spirit, if indeed they shall have been the temple of God, and the Spirit of God shall have dwelt in them, who breathes where he wills, and has diverse graces: Yet the knowledge of the one God is the possession of all the virtues.

*For all shall know. ((HIER.))* Because all shall be etc., *as far as* not in the nature in which he lay hidden in himself even when he was seen.

notes.text: Because — The practice of religion is the best way to understand it.
Taught me — By thy blessed spirit, illuminating my mind, and working upon my heart.
From whom — Even from me a teacher approved of God.

From an infant thou hast known the holy scriptures — Of the Old Testament. These only were extant when Timothy was an infant. Which are able to make thee wise unto salvation, through faith in the Messiah that was to come. How much more are the Old and New Testament together able, in God's hand, to make us more abundantly wise unto salvation! Even such a measure of present salvation as was not known before Jesus was glorified.

All scripture is inspired of God — The Spirit of God not only once inspired those who wrote it, but continually inspires, supernaturally assists, those that read it with earnest prayer. Hence it is so profitable for doctrine, for instruction of the ignorant, for the reproof or conviction of them that are in error or sin, for the correction or amendment of whatever is amiss, and for instructing or training up the children of God in all righteousness.
That the man of God — He that is united to and approved of God. May be perfect - Blameless himself, and throughly furnished - By the scripture, either to teach, reprove, correct, or train up others.
I charge thee therefore — This is deduced from the whole preceding chapter. At his appearing and his kingdom - That is, at his appearing in the kingdom of glory.

Be instant — Insist on, urge these things in season, out of season - That is, continually, at all times and places. It might be translated, with and without opportunity - Not only when a fair occasion is given: even when there is none, one must be made.

For they will heap up teachers — Therefore thou hast need of "all longsuffering." According to their own desires - Smooth as they can wish. Having itching ears - Fond of novelty and variety, which the number of new teachers, as well as their empty, soft, or philosophical discourses, pleased. Such teachers, and such hearers, seldom are much concerned with what is strict or to the purpose. Heap to themselves - Not enduring sound doctrine, they will reject the sound preachers, and gather together all that suit their own taste. Probably they send out one another as teachers, and so are never at a loss for numbers.

Watch — An earnest, constant, persevering exercise. The scripture watching, or waiting, implies steadfast faith, patient hope, labouring love, unceasing prayer; yea, the mighty exertion of all the affections of the soul that a man is capable of. In all things - Whatever you are doing, yet in that, and in all things, watch. Do the work of an evangelist - Which was next to that of an apostle.

glossa.text: *Thou hast known the holy scriptures which thee,* etc. He signifies that it profits much to have knowledge of the Old Testament, where the person of Christ and the incarnation is intimated, which avails unto the salvation of men.

*Out of season.* Thou actest in season, but thou seemest to be out of season to him who does not willingly hear, which nevertheless sometimes profits him. Do thou, however, knowing that this is in season for him which seems to him out of season, hold with a mild and modest mind the love and the care of his soundness. *Rebuke in all things.* To Timothy he urges a sharper patience. To Titus, who is too patient, he urges command.

*They will heap to themselves teachers.* That is, such as may teach them the things they wish. It is a prophecy of the holy Apostle, who, foreknowing things to come, commands that men be instant in doctrine, so that against that which was to come the Church might be prepared. For he says that such men shall be as wish to be taught according to their own desires, so that, namely, from teachers steadfast and truthful they may turn aside to those who will teach them the things which they willingly hear, because the truth will seem harsh to them, so that, true doctrine being forsaken, they may give themselves to fables.

*Do the work of an evangelist.* By testifying in work what thou art preaching with the mouth, that the mouth of the turtle-dove be twisted back to its wings, and that there be pomegranates and little bells upon the outermost edges of the hyacinth tunic.

notes.text: He spake a parable to them — This and the following parable warn us against two fatal extremes, with regard to prayer: the former against faintness and weariness, the latter against self confidence.

And shall not God — The most just Judge, vindicate his own elect - Preserve the Christians from all their adversaries, and in particular save them out of the general destruction, and avenge them of the Jews? Though he bear long with them - Though he does not immediately put an end, either to the wrongs of the wicked, or the sufferings of good men.

Yet when the Son of man cometh, will he find faith upon earth — Yet notwithstanding all the instances both of his long suffering and of his justice, whenever he shall remarkably appear, against their enemies in this age or in after ages, how few true believers will be found upon earth!

glossa.text: *A certain judge.* This parable exhorts to praying and to believing, and to presuming not upon ourselves but upon God.

*And a widow.* This widow can bear a likeness of the Church, which seems desolate until the Lord come, who nevertheless even now bears care for her in secret. *Avenge me.* Although the just are admonished to pray for their persecutors, yet, righteousness being safe, they seek this vengeance upon the evil: that all the evil may perish, either by being converted to righteousness, or by the loss through punishment of that power by which they now, against the good, so long as this very thing is expedient for the good, are able to do somewhat even temporally. And when the just desire this end to come, although they pray for their enemies, yet they are not absurdly said to desire vengeance.

*But yet.* I say that I will execute the vengeance of the just, but they will be exceedingly few, because when on the day of judgment I shall appear in the form of the Son of man, so great will be the rarity of the just that the ruin of the whole world must then be hastened, not so much for the cry of the faithful unjustly condemned, as for the torpor of those justly to be condemned. *Thinkest thou.* In the word the unbelief of doubting is rebuked; the Divinity does not form an opinion. For he through whom all things are knows all things, but by doubting he rebukes the hearts of the unbelieving.

notes.text: Very early in the morning, a great while before day. Jacob had helped his wives and children over the river, and he desired to be private, and was left alone, that he might again spread his cares and fears before God in prayer. While Jacob was earnest in prayer, stirring up himself to take hold on God, an angel takes hold on him. Some think this was a created angel, one of those that always behold the face of our Father. Rather it was the angel of the covenant, who often appeared in a human shape, before he assumed the human nature. We are told by the prophet, Hosea xii, 4, how Jacob wrestled, he wept and made supplication; prayers and tears were his weapons. It was not only a corporal, but a spiritual wrestling by vigourous faith and holy desire.

The angel prevailed not against him — That is, this discouragement did not shake his faith, nor silence his prayer. It was not in his own strength that he wrestled, nor by his own strength that he prevails; but by strength derived from heaven. That of Job illustrates this, Job xxiii, 6. Will he plead against me with his great power? No; had the angel done so, Jacob had been crushed; but he would put strength in me: and by that strength Jacob had power over the angel, Hosea xii, 3. The angel put out Jacob's thigh, to shew him what he could do, and that it was God he was wrestling with, for no man could disjoint his thigh with a touch. Some think that Jacob felt little or no pain from this hurt; it is probable be did not, for he did not so much as halt 'till the struggle was over, ver. 31, and if so, that was an evidence of a divine touch indeed, which wounded and healed at the same time.

Let me go — The angel, by an admirable condescension, speaks Jacob fair to let him go, as God said to Moses, Exod. xxxii, 10. Let me alone. Could not a mighty angel get clear of Jacob's grapples? He could; but thus he would put an honour upon Jacob's faith and prayer. The reason the angel gives why he would be gone is because the day breaks, and therefore he would not any longer detain Jacob, who had business to do, a journey to go, a family to look after. And he said, I will not let thee go except thou bless me - He resolves he will have a blessing, and rather shall all his bones be put out of joint, than he will go away without one. Those that would have the blessing of Christ must be in good earnest, and be importunate for it.

What is thy name? — Jacob (saith he) a supplanter, so Jacob signifies. Well, (faith the angel) be thou never so called any more: thou shalt be called Israel, a prince with God. He is a prince indeed, that is a prince with God; and those are truly honourable that are mighty, in prayer. Yet this was not all; having, power with God, he shall have power with men too; having prevailed for a blessing from heaven, he shall, no doubt, prevail for Esau's favour. Whatever enemies we have, if we can but make God our friend, we are well enough; they that by faith have power in heaven, have thereby as much power on earth as they have occasion for.

Wherefore dost thou ask after my name? — What good will it do thee to know that? The discovery of that was reserved for his death-bed, upon which he was taught to call him Shiloh. But instead of telling him his name, he gave him his blessing, which was the thing he wrestled for; he blessed him there, repeated and ratified the blessing formerly given him. See how wonderfully God condescends to countenance and crown importunate prayer? Those that resolve though God slay them, yet to trust in him, will at length be more than conquerors.
Peniel — That is, the face of God, because there he had seen the appearance of God, and obtained the favour of God.

He halted on his thigh — And some think he continued to do so to his dying day. If he did, he had no reason to complain, for the honour and comfort he obtained by his struggle was abundantly sufficient to countervail the damage, though he went limping to his grave. We read in the former chapter how Jacob had power with God, and prevailed; here we find what power he had with men too. Here is, I. A friendly meeting between Jacob and Esau, ver. 1-4. II. Their conference at their meeting. Their discourse is, (1.) About Jacob's family, ver. 5-7. (2.) About the present he had sent, ver. 8-11. (3.) About the progress of their journey, ver. 12-15. III. Jacob's settlement in Canaan, his house-ground, and altar, ver. 16-20.

glossa.text:
« I will appease him, » etc. These things are interposed by the writer. For it belongs not to a prudent man to uncover his art, and so to make himself suspected by those with whom he deals.

*((GREG. hom. 14, in Evang., tom. II.)) Mystically.* When Jacob returns to his own parents, etc., *as far as* that with inward sweetness we may lay hold of God.

« And behold a man, » etc. ((ISID. in Gen., tom. V.)) In this chiefly the image of the Lord's sacrament is figured, etc., *as far as* that it may no more be able to beget.

« By no means, he says, shall thy name be called Jacob, but, » etc. ((HIERON. in Q. Hebr. )) Josephus in the first book of the Antiquities, etc., *as far as* we are led rather by the authority of Scripture, and of the angel, or of God, who himself called him Israel, than by that of any secular eloquence.

« And Jacob called, » etc. That also which follows, « and he blessed him, and Jacob called the name of that place Phanuel, saying, » etc. In the Hebrew it is called « Phanuel, » that we may know it to be the same place which in the other volumes of Scripture, according to the Hebrews, is read *Phanuel.*

((GREG., lib. IV Moral., cap. 6.)) It is asked: since Truth says: « No man shall see my face; » And: « No man hath seen God at any time, » how does Jacob testify: « I saw the Lord face to face? » For human minds, the inward eye being purged, etc., *as far as* whence I Cor. XIII: « Then shall I know even as I am known. »

notes.text: Hills — To Sion and Moriah, which are called the holy mountains.
Shade — To keep thee from the burning heat of the sun.

Smite — With excessive heat. Moon - With that cold and moisture which come into the air by it. Intemperate heats and colds are the springs of many diseases. This psalm seems to have been wrote for the use of the people, when they came to Jerusalem at the three solemn feasts. David here shews the joy with which they were to go up to Jerusalem, ver. 1, 2. The esteem they were to have of it, ver. 3-5. The prayers they were to make for its welfare, ver, 6-9. A song of degrees of David.

glossa.text:
*A canticle of degrees.* ((CASS.)) The second degree, to seek the divine defence, against which nothing is shown to be able to prevail. ((AUG.)) For he upon whom, as he goes out of the world, dangers press, ought to demand the divine help, etc., *as far as* Such is this man, who lifts his eyes to God. ((CASS.)) First he lifts his eyes and prays: secondly, he affirms what he prayed for, showing the power of the help obtained.

*I have lifted up mine eyes.* ((ID.)) He who cried out as one bowed down, now taking breath, lifts his eyes to the holy intercessors.

*Neither let him slumber.* ((AUG.)) If faith sleeps in thee, Christ sleeps in thee.

((CASS.)) This is said after human custom; as when a weary watchman slumbers, he suffers theft.

((AUG.)) *Behold he shall not slumber.* Christ slumbers, etc., *as far as* but lest thou still suppose this of some man, he subjoins, *The Lord keepeth.*

*He that keepeth Israel.* ((AUG.)) He who cannot see the face, etc., *as far as* and for this man Christ does not sleep.

*The Lord keepeth.* ((CASS.)) The second part, where he affirms what he had prayed. And as if one should ask, Who is that keeper? he subjoins, *The Lord keepeth,* etc. ((AUG.)) It is not without cause, etc., *as far as* the love of God, namely, and of the neighbour.

*By day the sun shall not burn thee, nor the moon by night,* etc. ((ID.)) God is the sun, etc., *as far as* or *the moon,* that is, the Church, will not suffer thee to be burned in the night of tribulation. ((HIER.)) Or *by day* prosperity is understood, etc., *as far as* so now he keeps us both in prosperity and in adversity.

*May the Lord keep thy coming in.* ((CASS.)) He concludes all: to good beginnings may he join good endings. ((AUG.)) *May the Lord keep thy coming in.* He keeps those who enter, etc., *as far as* now unto eternity nothing shall hurt.

registers.label: Spare
lines: I lift up my eyes to the hills; from where will my help come?
We will not let you go until you bless us.
Jacob wrestled until the breaking of the day.
We will not let you go until you bless us.
Our help comes from the Lord, who keeps our going out and coming in.
Come, let us worship. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: All night by the river a man wrestles a stranger and will not quit, even limping, even spent.
We will not let you go until you bless us.
Pray like that, Jesus says — like the widow who wore down the judge — and do not lose heart.
We will not let you go until you bless us.
The Lord neither slumbers nor sleeps; he keeps watch over your life.
We will not let you go until you bless us.
So we come to worship holding on, lifting our eyes to the hills, asking and not giving up.
We will not let you go until you bless us!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: All night Jacob wrestles and will not quit.
We will not let you go until you bless us.
Pray like the widow; do not lose heart.
We will not let you go until you bless us.
Our help comes from the Lord, who never sleeps.
We will not let you go until you bless us. Amen.
